description: The settings that control how every AutoCAD command behaves: which object snaps are armed, whether dialogs appear, what units and scales new objects take, and what the current layer, colour and annotation scale are. Automation depends on them - a script or AutoLISP routine sets the variables it needs, does its work, and restores the user's values - and each one can be typed at the command prompt, set with SETVAR, read and written from AutoLISP with getvar/setvar, or driven through COM with GetVariable/SetVariable.

tools.name: OSMODE
tools.description: Holds the running object snaps as a bitcode: the sum of the weights of every snap mode currently armed. Object snaps override both picked and typed points, so a routine that draws at exact coordinates while OSMODE is non-zero can silently land points on nearby geometry instead of where it asked. Set it to 0 at the start of unattended work and restore the user's value at the end, or leave it alone and use a single-pick override for the few points that really need a snap.
tools.usage:
OSMODE <bitcode>
SETVAR OSMODE 175
(setvar "OSMODE" 175)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "OSMODE", 175   ; COM

parameters.description: No running object snaps at all - the value a batch routine normally wants.
Endpoint (END).
Midpoint (MID).
Center (CEN).
Node (NOD) - snaps to POINT objects and to the markers left by DIVIDE and MEASURE.
Quadrant (QUA).
Intersection (INT).
Insertion (INS) - insertion point of blocks, text and attributes.
Perpendicular (PER).
Tangent (TAN).
Nearest (NEA) - the snap most likely to spoil exact coordinate entry.
Geometric Center (GCE) of a closed polyline, spline or region, available from AutoCAD 2016; in earlier releases this bit was the obsolete Quick mode.
Apparent Intersection (APP) - where two objects would meet if extended, or cross in the current view.
Extension (EXT).
Parallel (PAR).

parameters.name: sum
parameters.description: Add the weights of the modes wanted: 175 = 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 32 + 128, the everyday drafting set.

tools.example:
; Script preamble for unattended drafting
OSMODE
0
ORTHOMODE
0

; AutoLISP: turn snaps off for the duration of a routine and put them back
(setq old-osmode (getvar "OSMODE"))
(setvar "OSMODE" 0)
(command "_LINE" '(0 0) '(100 0) "")
(setvar "OSMODE" old-osmode)
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing, so a template can carry the office default; the out-of-the-box initial value is 4133 (Endpoint + Center + Intersection + Extension). F3 toggles running snaps on and off interactively, and a snap typed at a point prompt (END, MID, CEN) or picked from Shift+right-click applies for that one pick only, which is what OSNAPOVERRIDE and the temporary override keys are for. Related: AUTOSNAP (marker, magnet and tooltips), APBOX (aperture box display), APERTURE (aperture size), OSNAPZ (force snapped points to the current elevation).

tools.name: PICKFIRST
tools.description: Controls whether objects can be selected before a command is started - noun-verb selection. With PICKFIRST 1 a selection made at the bare command prompt is handed to the next command, which is how grip editing and the Properties palette work. A routine that builds its own selection set with SELECT or ssget usually wants 0, so that a selection left over from the user is not silently picked up by the first command it issues.
tools.usage:
PICKFIRST <0 | 1>
SETVAR PICKFIRST 0
(setvar "PICKFIRST" 0)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "PICKFIRST", 0   ; COM

parameters.description: Objects must be selected after the command starts; a pre-selection is discarded.
A selection made before the command is passed to it (the default, and what grips need).

tools.example:
; Make a routine immune to whatever the user had selected
(setq old-pf (getvar "PICKFIRST"))
(setvar "PICKFIRST" 0)
(command "_.SELECT" "_ALL" "")
(setq ss (ssget "_P"))
(setvar "PICKFIRST" old-pf)
tools.notes: Saved in the registry, so it is a per-user setting rather than a property of the drawing. Related: PICKADD (whether selections accumulate), PICKAUTO (automatic window/crossing when picking empty space), PICKDRAG (click-drag windows), and (ssgetfirst)/(sssetfirst) which read and set the pre-selection from AutoLISP.

tools.name: PICKADD
tools.description: Controls whether each new pick adds to the selection set or replaces it. At 1 (the default) objects accumulate as you pick and Shift+pick removes them; at 0 each pick starts a new selection and Shift+pick is what adds. A drawing session where selections mysteriously vanish as soon as the next object is picked is almost always PICKADD set to 0 by a stray macro or the toggle button in the Properties palette.
tools.usage:
PICKADD <0 | 1 | 2>
SETVAR PICKADD 1
(setvar "PICKADD" 1)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "PICKADD", 1   ; COM

parameters.description: The most recent selection replaces the previous one; hold Shift to add objects.
Selections accumulate; hold Shift to remove objects from the set.
As 1, and in current releases the objects also stay selected after the command that used them ends.

tools.example:
; Restore sane selection behaviour at the start of a session file
PICKADD 1
PICKFIRST 1

; Read it before an interactive routine so the prompt text can match
(if (zerop (getvar "PICKADD"))
  (princ "\nHold SHIFT to add objects to the selection.")
)
tools.notes: Saved in the registry. The Properties palette has a small toggle button that writes this variable, which is how users change it without realising. Related: PICKFIRST, PICKSTYLE, SELECTIONPREVIEW and SELECTIONAREA (highlighting only, not set membership).

tools.name: PICKSTYLE
tools.description: Controls whether picking one member of a group selects the whole group, and whether picking an associative hatch also selects its boundary. It matters to automation because a routine written to modify a single object will happily modify every member of a group instead. Set it to 0 while a routine runs if it must treat objects individually, and restore the user's value afterwards.
tools.usage:
PICKSTYLE <0 | 1 | 2 | 3>
SETVAR PICKSTYLE 0
(setvar "PICKSTYLE" 0)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "PICKSTYLE", 0   ; COM

parameters.description: Neither group selection nor associative hatch selection.
Group selection: picking a member selects every object in the group.
Associative hatch selection: picking a hatch also selects its boundary objects.
Both group selection and associative hatch selection (the usual default).

tools.example:
; Edit individual objects even inside groups
(setq old-ps (getvar "PICKSTYLE"))
(setvar "PICKSTYLE" 0)
(command "_.CHPROP" (ssget "_X" '((8 . "WALLS"))) "" "_LA" "WALLS-NEW" "")
(setvar "PICKSTYLE" old-ps)
tools.notes: Ctrl+Shift+A toggles group selection on and off interactively, which is the same thing as switching the group bit of this variable. Related: GROUP and -GROUP (create and edit groups), GROUPDISPLAYMODE, HPASSOC (whether new hatches are associative at all).

tools.name: CMDECHO
tools.description: Controls whether the prompts and the input of a command issued from AutoLISP are echoed to the command line. Set it to 0 inside a routine so the user sees only the messages the routine chooses to print instead of a wall of prompts scrolling past, and set it back to 1 before returning. It is not saved between sessions, but a routine that aborts with CMDECHO 0 leaves the whole session silent, so restore it in an error handler as well as on the normal exit path.
tools.usage:
CMDECHO <0 | 1>
SETVAR CMDECHO 0
(setvar "CMDECHO" 0)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "CMDECHO", 0   ; COM

parameters.description: Command prompts and input issued by (command ...) are not echoed.
Everything is echoed to the command line, the default and the state to leave behind.

tools.example:
(defun c:QUIETMOVE ( / old-echo old-err)
  (setq old-echo (getvar "CMDECHO"))
  (setq old-err *error*)
  (defun *error* (msg)
    (setvar "CMDECHO" old-echo)
    (setq *error* old-err)
    (princ (strcat "\nCancelled: " msg))
  )
  (setvar "CMDECHO" 0)
  (command "_.MOVE" (ssget) "" '(0 0) '(100 0))
  (setvar "CMDECHO" old-echo)
  (setq *error* old-err)
  (princ)
)
tools.notes: Not saved - every session starts at 1. It affects the echo only, not whether the command runs, and it does not silence error messages. Related: NOMUTT (suppresses the ordinary status messages as well), MENUECHO (menu and macro echo), and (vl-cmdf) as an alternative to (command) that validates its arguments.

tools.name: FILEDIA
tools.description: Controls whether commands that read or write files show a file dialog or ask for the path on the command line. Every script that opens, saves, exports, plots to a file, inserts from a DWG or loads a linetype must set FILEDIA 0 first: otherwise a modal dialog opens and the script stops dead waiting for a human. With FILEDIA 0 you can still force the dialog for a single prompt by answering it with a tilde.
tools.usage:
FILEDIA <0 | 1>
SETVAR FILEDIA 0
(setvar "FILEDIA" 0)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "FILEDIA", 0   ; COM

parameters.description: No file dialogs; file names are typed at the command line. Mandatory for scripts and batch work.
File dialogs appear as normal (the default).
Typed at a file name prompt while FILEDIA is 0, it forces the dialog for that one prompt.

tools.example:
; Batch export: suppress every dialog, then work silently
FILEDIA 0
ATTDIA 0
CMDECHO 0
-WBLOCK
C:/output/VALVE_GATE.dwg
VALVE_GATE
FILEDIA 1
tools.notes: Saved in the registry, so a script that leaves it at 0 makes the application feel broken for the user afterwards - always set it back. It does not suppress non-file dialogs; those need CMDDIA, ATTDIA, EXPERT, or the hyphen-prefixed form of the command (-LAYER, -INSERT, -PLOT).

tools.name: ATTDIA
tools.description: Controls whether INSERT asks for attribute values in the Edit Attributes dialog or at the command line. Scripted insertion of title blocks and tagged symbols needs ATTDIA 0, so that the values can simply be the next lines of the script; with ATTDIA 1 the dialog opens and the script stalls. It has no effect when ATTREQ is 0, because then no values are asked for at all.
tools.usage:
ATTDIA <0 | 1>
SETVAR ATTDIA 0
(setvar "ATTDIA" 0)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "ATTDIA", 0   ; COM

parameters.description: Attribute values are prompted for one at a time on the command line.
The Edit Attributes dialog is displayed (the interactive default).

tools.example:
ATTDIA 0
ATTREQ 1
FILEDIA 0
-INSERT
TITLEBLOCK_A1=C:/standards/blocks/TB_A1.dwg
0,0
1
1
0
PROJECT 1042
REV C
J. DOE
tools.notes: Saved in the registry. The prompts appear in the order the attribute definitions were selected when the block was made - BATTMAN reorders them, and getting that order wrong is the usual reason a scripted insert puts the drawing number in the date field. Related: ATTREQ, ATTMODE/ATTDISP (visibility), EATTEDIT and -ATTEDIT (editing values afterwards).

tools.name: ATTREQ
tools.description: Controls whether attribute values are asked for at all when a block is inserted. At 0, every attribute silently takes the default value stored in its definition and no prompt of any kind appears, which is what you want when the values will be filled in afterwards by LISP, by a data extraction round-trip or by ATTSYNC. At 1 the values are requested, either in a dialog or on the command line depending on ATTDIA.
tools.usage:
ATTREQ <0 | 1>
SETVAR ATTREQ 0
(setvar "ATTREQ" 0)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "ATTREQ", 0   ; COM

parameters.description: No prompting; every attribute uses the default defined by ATTDEF.
Attribute values are requested on insertion (the default).

tools.example:
; Drop 200 symbols quickly, then write the tags with LISP
ATTREQ 0
ATTDIA 0
-INSERT
EQUIP_TAG
1200,850
1
1
0

; Fill the values afterwards
(vlax-for att (vlax-invoke (vlax-ename->vla-object (entlast)) 'GetAttributes)
  (if (= (vla-get-TagString att) "TAG_NO") (vla-put-TextString att "P-101"))
)
tools.notes: Saved in the registry. ATTREQ 0 combined with ATTDIA 0 makes insertion completely silent, which is the standard batch setting. Constant attributes are never prompted for whatever the value is. Related: ATTDIA, ATTSYNC (push definition changes to existing insertions), DATAEXTRACTION.

tools.name: EXPERT
tools.description: Suppresses successive levels of the 'are you sure' confirmation prompts that stop an unattended script dead. Each higher value suppresses everything the lower values do plus one more class of question, and a suppressed prompt is answered as though you had agreed. Raise it only around the operation that needs it and put it back to 0 immediately, because at level 2 and above it will overwrite files and redefine blocks without a word.
tools.usage:
EXPERT <0-5>
SETVAR EXPERT 2
(setvar "EXPERT" 2)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "EXPERT", 2   ; COM

parameters.description: All prompts are issued normally (the default and the state to restore).
Suppresses 'About to regen, proceed?' and 'Really want to turn the current layer off?'.
Also suppresses the block redefinition prompt of BLOCK and the overwrite prompt when saving or writing over an existing file.
Also suppresses the LINETYPE prompts about reloading or redefining a linetype that is already loaded.
Also suppresses the overwrite prompts of the UCS Save and VPORTS Save options.
Also suppresses the redefine prompt of the -DIMSTYLE Save option.

tools.example:
; Redefine a standard block in every drawing of a batch without being asked
EXPERT 2
FILEDIA 0
-INSERT
TITLEBLOCK_A1=C:/standards/blocks/TB_A1.dwg

EXPERT 0
FILEDIA 1
QSAVE
tools.notes: Not saved - it starts every session at 0, which is the only reason a forgotten EXPERT 5 is not permanently dangerous. It suppresses prompts, it does not change what the command does. Related: FILEDIA and ATTDIA (dialogs rather than prompts), CMDDIA, and the hyphen-prefixed command forms.

tools.name: NOMUTT
tools.description: Controls the ordinary running commentary - the 'muttering' - that AutoCAD writes to the command line while a command works. At 0, messages display normally; at 1 they are suppressed except where a dialog or a command genuinely requires them. Use it with CMDECHO when a routine should leave a clean transcript, for example one that loops over hundreds of objects and prints a single summary line at the end.
tools.usage:
NOMUTT <0 | 1>
SETVAR NOMUTT 1
(setvar "NOMUTT" 1)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "NOMUTT", 1   ; COM

parameters.description: Normal message display (the default).
Suppresses the ordinary message display.

tools.example:
(setq old-mutt (getvar "NOMUTT") old-echo (getvar "CMDECHO"))
(setvar "NOMUTT" 1)
(setvar "CMDECHO" 0)
(setq n 0)
(foreach lay '("WALLS" "DOORS" "GLAZING")
  (command "_.-LAYER" "_M" lay "")
  (setq n (1+ n))
)
(setvar "CMDECHO" old-echo)
(setvar "NOMUTT" old-mutt)
(princ (strcat "\n" (itoa n) " layers created."))
tools.notes: Not saved between sessions. Like CMDECHO it must be restored in an error handler, or the command line stays mute for the rest of the session and the user assumes the application has hung. Related: CMDECHO, MENUECHO, LOGFILEMODE (write the command line history to a file for a batch log).

tools.name: SECURELOAD
tools.description: Controls where executable code - AutoLISP, ARX and DBX modules, VBA projects and .NET assemblies - may be loaded from. It exists because a DWG can carry or reference code, so opening a drawing from outside the organisation can otherwise run someone else's routine. Deployment that ships LISP tools alongside a drawing set must put the code on a trusted path rather than turning this down.
tools.usage:
SECURELOAD <0 | 1 | 2>
SETVAR SECURELOAD 1
(setvar "SECURELOAD" 1)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "SECURELOAD", 1   ; COM

parameters.description: Executable files load from anywhere with no warning - not a setting to leave in place.
Files on a trusted path load silently; anything else raises a warning that the user must accept (the default).
Only files on a trusted path load at all; everything else is refused outright.

tools.example:
; Deployment step: trust the standards folder, then tighten the setting
(setvar "TRUSTEDPATHS" "C:/standards/lisp;C:/standards/tools")
(setvar "SECURELOAD" 2)
(load "C:/standards/lisp/office-tools.lsp")
tools.notes: Saved in the registry, per user profile. A folder that ordinary users can write to is not accepted as genuinely trusted, which is deliberate - a writable trusted folder defeats the whole mechanism. Related: TRUSTEDPATHS, TRUSTEDDOMAINS, LEGACYCODESEARCH (whether the drawing's own folder is searched for code), ACADLSPASDOC and acaddoc.lsp.

tools.name: TRUSTEDPATHS
tools.description: Holds the list of folders from which executable files are loaded without the security warning raised by SECURELOAD, as a single string of paths separated by semicolons. Setting it is the correct way to deploy a company LISP or .NET toolset: one trusted, non-user-writable folder, set once in the deployment, instead of loosening SECURELOAD on every workstation. Reading it tells a deployment script whether its folder has already been trusted.
tools.usage:
TRUSTEDPATHS <"path;path">
SETVAR TRUSTEDPATHS "C:/standards/lisp;C:/standards/tools"
(setvar "TRUSTEDPATHS" "C:/standards/lisp;C:/standards/tools")   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "TRUSTEDPATHS", "C:/standards/lisp"   ; COM

parameters.name: path list
parameters.description: One or more folder paths separated by semicolons; the whole list is replaced when you set the variable, so append to the existing value rather than overwriting it.

parameters.name: "" (empty)
parameters.description: No trusted folders - with SECURELOAD 2 that means no external code can be loaded at all.

tools.example:
; Append a folder without discarding what is already trusted
(setq tp (getvar "TRUSTEDPATHS"))
(if (not (vl-string-search "standards/lisp" tp))
  (setvar "TRUSTEDPATHS"
    (if (= tp "") "C:/standards/lisp" (strcat tp ";C:/standards/lisp")))
)
(princ (getvar "TRUSTEDPATHS"))
tools.notes: Saved in the registry, per user profile; it is the same list shown as Trusted Locations in the Options dialog. Folders that ordinary users can write to may be rejected or still warn, by design. Related: SECURELOAD, TRUSTEDDOMAINS (web locations), and the support file search path, which is a separate list that decides where files are found rather than whether they are trusted.

tools.name: INSUNITS
tools.description: Declares the units the current drawing is drawn in, which decides the automatic scale factor applied when a block, an xref or a DesignCenter or tool palette item is inserted from a drawing with different units. A block drawn in inches and inserted into a millimetre drawing is scaled by 25.4 automatically when both drawings declare their units, and arrives comically wrong when one of them does not. Set it in the template so every new drawing agrees.
tools.usage:
INSUNITS <code>
SETVAR INSUNITS 4
(setvar "INSUNITS" 4)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "INSUNITS", 4   ; COM

parameters.description: Unitless - no automatic scaling is applied on insertion.
Inches.
Feet.
Miles.
Millimetres - the usual value for metric mechanical and building drawings.
Centimetres.
Metres.
Kilometres.
Microinches, mils and yards; the enumeration continues through angstroms, nanometers, microns, decimeters and larger units for the values above.

tools.example:
; Template preamble for a metric drawing
INSUNITS 4
MEASUREMENT 1
LUNITS 2

; Check before inserting a library block
(if (/= (getvar "INSUNITS") 4)
  (princ "\nWarning: drawing is not set to millimetres - blocks may be scaled.")
)
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing. INSUNITSDEFSOURCE and INSUNITSDEFTARGET (both in the registry) supply the assumed units when one of the two drawings is unitless. The BLOCK command's Block unit setting records the same information inside a block definition. Note that INSUNITS is independent of LUNITS, which is only a display format, and of MEASUREMENT, which only selects the hatch and linetype files.

tools.name: MEASUREMENT
tools.description: Selects which hatch pattern and linetype definition files the current drawing uses: the imperial files acad.pat and acad.lin, or the metric files acadiso.pat and acadiso.lin. The metric pattern and linetype definitions are roughly 25.4 times larger, so a millimetre drawing left at the imperial setting is exactly why dashed lines plot solid and hatches come out as a black smear. MEASUREINIT holds the same choice in the registry and decides what a drawing started from scratch gets.
tools.usage:
MEASUREMENT <0 | 1>
SETVAR MEASUREMENT 1
(setvar "MEASUREMENT" 1)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "MEASUREMENT", 1   ; COM

parameters.description: Imperial: acad.lin and acad.pat are used for linetypes and hatch patterns.
Metric: acadiso.lin and acadiso.pat are used.

parameters.name: MEASUREINIT
parameters.description: The registry counterpart, with the same two values, applied to drawings created from scratch rather than from a template.

tools.example:
; Fix an imported drawing that is metric but was set up imperial
MEASUREMENT 1
FILEDIA 0
-LINETYPE
L
HIDDEN
acadiso.lin


LTSCALE 1
REGEN
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing (MEASUREINIT is saved in the registry). It changes only which definition files are used as the source - it does not convert existing objects, change the drawing units, or touch INSUNITS, and linetypes already loaded keep the definitions they were loaded with. Related: INSUNITS, LTSCALE, HPNAME and HPSCALE.

tools.name: LUNITS
tools.description: Sets the linear unit format used to display coordinates, distances and areas, and to interpret what is typed at a distance prompt. Engineering and Architectural formats are feet-and-inches notations that assume one drawing unit is one inch, so switching to them in a millimetre drawing produces nonsense. Set it in the template, together with the precision, rather than per drawing.
tools.usage:
LUNITS <1-5>
SETVAR LUNITS 2
(setvar "LUNITS" 2)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "LUNITS", 2   ; COM

parameters.description: Scientific, for example 1.55E+02.
Decimal - the metric default.
Engineering: feet and decimal inches; one drawing unit is one inch.
Architectural: feet and fractional inches; one drawing unit is one inch.
Fractional.

parameters.name: LUPREC
parameters.description: The companion variable holding the number of decimal places, or the fractional denominator, used with the chosen format.

tools.example:
; Metric drawing, two decimal places
LUNITS 2
LUPREC 2

; Format a number the way the drawing displays it
(princ (rtos 152.4 (getvar "LUNITS") (getvar "LUPREC")))
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing; the UNITS command sets this and its relatives in one dialog, and -UNITS is the command-line form for scripts. It affects display and the strings returned by rtos, never the stored geometry. Related: LUPREC, AUNITS and AUPREC for angles, INSUNITS for insertion scaling, DIMLUNIT and DIMDEC which give dimension text its own independent format.

tools.name: AUNITS
tools.description: Sets the angular unit format used to display angles and to interpret angles typed at a prompt. This is a real trap in automation: a macro that answers an angle prompt with 45 gets 45 radians rather than 45 degrees if the drawing is set to radians, and surveyor's units expect bearings such as N45d0'0"E. Check it, or set it explicitly, before a routine feeds angles to commands.
tools.usage:
AUNITS <0-4>
SETVAR AUNITS 0
(setvar "AUNITS" 0)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "AUNITS", 0   ; COM

parameters.description: Decimal degrees (the default).
Degrees, minutes and seconds.
Gradians.
Radians.
Surveyor's units - quadrant bearings such as N45d0'0"E.

parameters.name: AUPREC
parameters.description: The companion precision variable for the chosen angular format.

tools.example:
; Force decimal degrees around a routine that types angles
(setq old-au (getvar "AUNITS"))
(setvar "AUNITS" 0)
(command "_.ROTATE" (ssget) "" '(0 0) 30)
(setvar "AUNITS" old-au)

; AutoLISP angle functions are always in radians whatever AUNITS says
(setq a (angle '(0 0) '(100 100)))   ; 0.785398
(princ (angtos a (getvar "AUNITS") (getvar "AUPREC")))
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing. The AutoLISP functions angle, polar, sin and cos always work in radians regardless of AUNITS; angtos and angtof convert to and from the display format. Related: AUPREC, ANGBASE (direction of zero degrees) and ANGDIR (clockwise or counter-clockwise), which shift every angle in the drawing and are a second common source of rotated output.

tools.name: DIMSCALE
tools.description: Overall scale factor applied to every size in a dimension style - text height, arrowhead size, extension line offset, gaps - without changing the measured value. In a drawing plotted at 1:50 that wants 2.5 mm text, DIMSCALE 50 is what makes dimensions come out the right size on paper. Setting it to 0 makes dimensions created inside a layout viewport scale themselves by that viewport's zoom factor instead, which is the older alternative to annotative styles.
tools.usage:
DIMSCALE <value>
SETVAR DIMSCALE 50
(setvar "DIMSCALE" 50.0)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "DIMSCALE", 50#   ; COM

parameters.description: Scale is computed from the zoom factor of the layout viewport the dimension is created in; in model space it behaves as 1.
Multiplier applied to all the size settings of the dimension style - normally the reciprocal of the plot scale (50 for 1:50).

tools.example:
; Set up for a 1:50 sheet, then push the change onto existing dimensions
DIMSCALE 50
-DIMSTYLE
S
ISO-25-50

SELECT ALL

-DIMSTYLE
A
P
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing. It is one of the DIM family of variables, all of which are captured into a named style by -DIMSTYLE Save and applied to existing dimensions by -DIMSTYLE Apply or DIMSTYLE Update. Annotative dimension styles ignore DIMSCALE entirely and take their size from the annotation scale in CANNOSCALE. Related: LTSCALE and the text height in the style, which must be scaled the same way if they are not annotative.

tools.name: LTSCALE
tools.description: Global linetype scale: the dash pattern of every dashed, dotted, centre and phantom line in the drawing is multiplied by it. It is the first thing to check when linetypes plot as continuous lines (the value is far too small for the drawing) or as one endless dash (far too large); a common starting point is the plot scale, adjusted for whether the drawing uses the imperial or the ISO linetype definitions. A REGEN is needed before the change is visible.
tools.usage:
LTSCALE <value>
SETVAR LTSCALE 25
(setvar "LTSCALE" 25.0)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "LTSCALE", 25#   ; COM

parameters.description: Multiplier applied to every linetype pattern in the drawing; it must be positive and non-zero.

parameters.name: effective scale
parameters.description: An object's actual dash length is its own linetype scale (CELTSCALE when it was created, or the Linetype scale property) multiplied by LTSCALE.

tools.example:
; Standardise linetype scale across a batch of drawings
LTSCALE 25
PSLTSCALE 1
MSLTSCALE 1
REGENALL

; Report the effective scale of the last object created
(princ (* (getvar "LTSCALE")
          (cdr (assoc 48 (entget (entlast))))))
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing. Changing it affects every object at once - to change one object use its Linetype scale property instead. The ISO linetype definitions in acadiso.lin are already sized in millimetres, so metric drawings usually need a much smaller LTSCALE than the plot scale suggests. Related: CELTSCALE (scale given to new objects), PSLTSCALE, MSLTSCALE, MEASUREMENT (which linetype file is used).

tools.name: PSLTSCALE
tools.description: Controls whether linetype dash lengths in a layout are measured in paper space units (1) or in the drawing units of the model geometry (0). With PSLTSCALE 1 a dashed line looks identical in every viewport no matter what each viewport is zoomed to, which is exactly what a sheet holding views at 1:50 and 1:5 side by side needs. Change it and then REGENALL, or the old display lingers.
tools.usage:
PSLTSCALE <0 | 1>
SETVAR PSLTSCALE 1
(setvar "PSLTSCALE" 1)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "PSLTSCALE", 1   ; COM

parameters.description: Dash lengths follow the model space units of the geometry, so the same linetype looks different in viewports at different scales.
Dash lengths are scaled to paper space units, giving a consistent appearance across viewports (the default).

tools.example:
; Sheet set-up: one LTSCALE for every viewport scale
PSLTSCALE 1
LTSCALE 1
REGENALL

(setvar "PSLTSCALE" 1)
(command "_.REGENALL")
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing. It applies to objects displayed through a layout viewport, not to the Model tab - MSLTSCALE is the model space counterpart. Objects drawn directly in paper space are always in paper units anyway. Related: LTSCALE, MSLTSCALE, CELTSCALE.

tools.name: MSLTSCALE
tools.description: Controls whether linetypes shown on the Model tab are scaled by the current annotation scale (1) or not (0). It lets a single LTSCALE value serve several annotation scales, so switching the model space annotation scale from 1:50 to 1:5 keeps dashes looking sensible. Drawings created in releases before annotative scaling open with it at 0, so an old file whose linetypes suddenly change appearance is usually an MSLTSCALE difference; REGEN after changing it.
tools.usage:
MSLTSCALE <0 | 1>
SETVAR MSLTSCALE 1
(setvar "MSLTSCALE" 1)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "MSLTSCALE", 1   ; COM

parameters.description: Model space linetypes are not scaled by the annotation scale - the behaviour of drawings from older releases.
Model space linetypes are scaled by the current annotation scale (the default in new drawings).

tools.example:
; Bring an inherited drawing in line with the office template
MSLTSCALE 1
PSLTSCALE 1
LTSCALE 1
CANNOSCALE
1:50
REGEN
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing. A REGEN is required for the new setting to show. Because it multiplies by the annotation scale, a drawing that already has a hand-tuned LTSCALE will look wrong the moment MSLTSCALE is turned on - adjust LTSCALE at the same time. Related: LTSCALE, PSLTSCALE, CANNOSCALE.

tools.name: CLAYER
tools.description: Holds the name of the current layer, which is the layer every new object is created on. Setting it is the reliable way for a routine to put geometry where it belongs: create or verify the layer with -LAYER first, set CLAYER, draw, then restore the previous value. Assigning a layer that does not exist, or one that is frozen or frozen in the current viewport, fails and leaves the current layer unchanged.
tools.usage:
CLAYER <"layer name">
SETVAR CLAYER "DIMENSIONS"
(setvar "CLAYER" "DIMENSIONS")   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "CLAYER", "DIMENSIONS"   ; COM

parameters.name: layer name
parameters.description: Name of an existing, thawed layer. Layer names are not case sensitive and may contain spaces.
Layer 0, the layer block geometry should normally be drawn on so that insertions inherit properties.

tools.example:
; Script: create the layer if needed and make it current
-LAYER
M
DIMENSIONS
C
2



; AutoLISP: draw on a layer and put the user's layer back
(setq old-lay (getvar "CLAYER"))
(setvar "CLAYER" "DIMENSIONS")
(command "_.DIMLINEAR" '(0 0) '(100 0) '(0 -20))
(setvar "CLAYER" old-lay)
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing. -LAYER Make (M) both creates and sets the current layer in one step, which is shorter than -LAYER New followed by setting CLAYER, and is safe when the layer already exists. Related: CECOLOR, CELTYPE and CELWEIGHT, which should normally stay at BYLAYER so that objects inherit from here; CMLJUST and the layer overrides in HPLAYER and the dimension DIMLAYER.

tools.name: CECOLOR
tools.description: Sets the colour given to new objects. It accepts BYLAYER, BYBLOCK, an index colour from 1 to 255 (or its name, such as red), and a true colour written in the RGB:r,g,b form. Production drawings should leave it at BYLAYER so that colour is controlled by layer and by plot style; set it explicitly only when a routine must create an object of a fixed colour, and set it back afterwards.
tools.usage:
CECOLOR <"BYLAYER" | "BYBLOCK" | "1"-"255" | "RGB:r,g,b">
SETVAR CECOLOR BYLAYER
(setvar "CECOLOR" "1")   ; AutoLISP - note the value is a string
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "CECOLOR", "1"   ; COM

parameters.name: BYLAYER
parameters.description: New objects take the colour of the layer they are created on (the normal production setting).

parameters.name: BYBLOCK
parameters.description: New objects are drawn white/black until they are put in a block, then take the colour of the block reference - how block geometry should be drawn.

parameters.name: 1 to 255
parameters.description: An AutoCAD Color Index number; 1 red, 2 yellow, 3 green, 4 cyan, 5 blue, 6 magenta, 7 white/black.

parameters.name: RGB:r,g,b
parameters.description: A true colour, for example RGB:255,0,0.

tools.example:
; Draw a temporary construction object in red, then restore
(setq old-col (getvar "CECOLOR"))
(setvar "CECOLOR" "1")
(command "_.CIRCLE" '(0 0) 5.0)
(setvar "CECOLOR" old-col)

; Script form
CECOLOR
RGB:0,128,255
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing; the value is always a string, even for the index numbers, which catches out COM and LISP code that passes an integer. Objects already created keep their colour - SETBYLAYER is the command that retro-fits BYLAYER onto geometry created with hard-coded colours. Related: CELTYPE, CELWEIGHT, CETRANSPARENCY.

tools.name: CELTYPE
tools.description: Sets the linetype given to new objects: BYLAYER, BYBLOCK, or the name of a linetype that has already been loaded into the drawing. Assigning a linetype that has not been loaded simply fails, so a script must load it first with -LINETYPE from acad.lin or acadiso.lin - with FILEDIA 0 so the file dialog does not appear. As with colour, production work leaves this at BYLAYER.
tools.usage:
CELTYPE <"BYLAYER" | "BYBLOCK" | "linetype name">
SETVAR CELTYPE HIDDEN
(setvar "CELTYPE" "HIDDEN")   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "CELTYPE", "HIDDEN"   ; COM

parameters.name: BYLAYER
parameters.description: New objects take the linetype of their layer (the normal setting).

parameters.name: BYBLOCK
parameters.description: New objects inherit the linetype of the block reference they end up inside.

parameters.name: linetype name
parameters.description: Any linetype already loaded in the drawing, for example CONTINUOUS, HIDDEN, CENTER, DASHED, or their ISO equivalents such as HIDDEN2 and ACAD_ISO02W100.

tools.example:
; Load a linetype and use it, script form
FILEDIA 0
-LINETYPE
L
HIDDEN
acadiso.lin


CELTYPE
HIDDEN
LINE
0,0
100,0

CELTYPE
BYLAYER
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing. CELTSCALE sets the per-object linetype scale of new objects, and the object's final dash length is CELTSCALE multiplied by LTSCALE. MEASUREMENT decides whether acad.lin or acadiso.lin is the default source file. Related: CECOLOR, CELWEIGHT, LTSCALE, PSLTSCALE.

tools.name: CELWEIGHT
tools.description: Sets the lineweight given to new objects. Negative values are the three symbolic settings - ByLayer, ByBlock and Default - and any other value is a lineweight in hundredths of a millimetre taken from the fixed list of supported widths. Values that are not on that list are rejected, so a routine must choose from the list rather than converting an arbitrary millimetre figure.
tools.usage:
CELWEIGHT <-3 | -2 | -1 | supported value>
SETVAR CELWEIGHT 50
(setvar "CELWEIGHT" 50)   ; AutoLISP - 50 means 0.50 mm
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "CELWEIGHT", 50   ; COM

parameters.description: ByLayer - the normal production setting.
ByBlock.
Default, meaning the value held in LWDEFAULT.

tools.example:
; Heavy outline, then back to ByLayer
(setq old-lw (getvar "CELWEIGHT"))
(setvar "CELWEIGHT" 70)          ; 0.70 mm
(command "_.PLINE" '(0 0) '(100 0) '(100 50) '(0 50) "_C")
(setvar "CELWEIGHT" old-lw)      ; usually -1, ByLayer
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing. LWDISPLAY controls whether lineweights are shown on screen at all - a drawing can be perfectly set up and still look uniform because LWDISPLAY is off - and LWUNITS switches the display between millimetres and inches. Plot style tables can override lineweight at plot time, so a drawing using an STB or CTB may ignore these values entirely. Related: CECOLOR, CELTYPE, LWDEFAULT.

tools.name: TEXTSTYLE
tools.description: Holds the name of the current text style, used by TEXT, MTEXT, dimensions that do not override it, and any routine that creates text. Setting the variable is cleaner than answering the Style option inside every command, and it must name a style that already exists in the drawing - create it first with -STYLE. If the style has a fixed (non-zero) height, the height prompt disappears from TEXT and MTEXT, which changes how many answers a script has to supply.
tools.usage:
TEXTSTYLE <"style name">
SETVAR TEXTSTYLE NOTES
(setvar "TEXTSTYLE" "NOTES")   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "TEXTSTYLE", "NOTES"   ; COM

parameters.name: style name
parameters.description: Name of a text style defined in the drawing; Standard always exists.

parameters.name: fixed height styles
parameters.description: A style whose height is not 0 suppresses the height prompt in TEXT and MTEXT, so scripts written for a variable-height style break against it.

parameters.name: annotative styles
parameters.description: Take the paper height from the style and the scale from CANNOSCALE, so TEXTSIZE and DIMSCALE do not apply.

tools.example:
; Create the style, then use it, script form
FILEDIA 0
-STYLE
NOTES
isocp.shx
0
1
0
N
N

TEXTSTYLE
NOTES
TEXT
J
MC
100,50
2.5
0
PUMP ROOM
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing. TEXTSIZE holds the default text height used when the current style's height is 0, and is what TEXT offers as its default. -STYLE is the script-safe form of the STYLE command. Related: CANNOSCALE for annotative text, MIRRTEXT, DIMTXSTY (the text style used by dimensions), and the FONTALT/FONTMAP settings that substitute fonts that cannot be found.

tools.name: MIRRTEXT
tools.description: Controls what MIRROR does to text, attributes and attribute definitions. At 0, the default, text is moved to its mirrored position but stays readable; at 1 it is reflected like any other geometry and comes out back to front. Set it to 0 before any batch mirroring of drawings that contain annotation, and to 1 only when a genuinely reversed image is wanted, such as a stencil or a reverse-reading mark.
tools.usage:
MIRRTEXT <0 | 1>
SETVAR MIRRTEXT 0
(setvar "MIRRTEXT" 0)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "MIRRTEXT", 0   ; COM

parameters.description: Text is repositioned by MIRROR but remains readable (the default).
Text is mirrored with the rest of the geometry and reads backwards.

tools.example:
; Mirror a whole assembly and keep the labels readable
MIRRTEXT 0
MIRROR
ALL

0,0
0,100
N

; From AutoLISP
(setvar "MIRRTEXT" 0)
(command "_.MIRROR" (ssget "_X") "" '(0 0) '(0 100) "_N")
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing. It is read at the moment MIRROR runs, so it cannot repair text that has already been reversed - mirror that text again with the correct setting, or reset its rotation. Blocks follow the same rule for the text inside them. Related: TEXTSTYLE, and the Backwards and Upside down flags of a text style, which are separate settings that survive mirroring.

tools.name: PDMODE
tools.description: Sets how POINT objects are drawn. The base value chooses the marker - 0 a dot, 1 nothing at all, 2 a cross, 3 an X, 4 a vertical tick - and adding 32, 64 or 96 draws a circle, a square, or both around it. Points are invisible at 1 and nearly invisible at 0, so a routine that relies on DIVIDE, MEASURE or surveyed points should set a visible style first or the markers appear to be missing.
tools.usage:
PDMODE <value>
SETVAR PDMODE 35
(setvar "PDMODE" 35)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "PDMODE", 35   ; COM

parameters.description: A single dot at the point.
Nothing is displayed - the point still exists and Node snap still finds it.
A cross through the point.
An X through the point.
A short vertical tick upwards from the point.
Add 32 to draw a circle around the marker, 64 for a square, 96 for both; so 35 is an X inside a circle.

parameters.name: PDSIZE
parameters.description: The companion size variable: 0 means 5 percent of the graphics area, a positive value is an absolute size in drawing units, a negative value is a percentage of the viewport so markers stay visible at any zoom.

tools.example:
; Visible markers before setting out fixing points
PDMODE 35
PDSIZE -3
DIVIDE
(select the arc)
8
REGEN

; Snap to the results
OSMODE 8
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing. Existing points only take on a new style after a REGEN, which is why a change often appears to have done nothing. DDPTYPE opens the dialog that sets both variables. Related: PDSIZE, the Node (NOD) object snap in OSMODE, and the DIVIDE and MEASURE commands that create points in quantity.

tools.name: FILLMODE
tools.description: Controls whether 2D solids, wide polylines, donuts, hatches and gradient fills are displayed and plotted filled (1) or drawn as outlines only (0). Turning it off speeds up regeneration and panning in a drawing crowded with solid fills, and turning it back on before plotting is essential or the sheet comes out hollow. A REGEN is required after changing it.
tools.usage:
FILLMODE <0 | 1>
SETVAR FILLMODE 1
(setvar "FILLMODE" 1)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "FILLMODE", 1   ; COM

parameters.description: Filled objects are shown and plotted as outlines only.
Filled objects are displayed and plotted filled (the default).

tools.example:
; Speed up editing on a heavily hatched drawing, then restore for plotting
FILLMODE 0
REGEN

; ... editing ...

FILLMODE 1
REGEN
-PLOT
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing. FILL and FILL OFF are the command form of the same setting. It affects 2D filled objects only - 3D solids, shaded views and rendered output are unaffected. Related: HPNAME/HPSCALE for the hatches it hides, TEXTFILL (filled TrueType text in plots), and QTEXT which does the equivalent job for text.

tools.name: HPNAME
tools.description: Holds the default hatch pattern name offered by HATCH and -HATCH, for example ANSI31, SOLID, NET or AR-CONC. Setting HPNAME, HPSCALE and HPANG before calling -HATCH means the script has fewer prompts to answer and is much less likely to break when a release changes the prompt sequence. Set it to a single dot or an empty string for no default pattern.
tools.usage:
HPNAME <"pattern name">
SETVAR HPNAME ANSI31
(setvar "HPNAME" "ANSI31")   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "HPNAME", "ANSI31"   ; COM

parameters.name: pattern name
parameters.description: Any pattern defined in the .pat files on the support path, or a custom pattern file name.

parameters.name: SOLID
parameters.description: The solid fill pattern - the only one whose appearance does not depend on HPSCALE.

parameters.name: "." or ""
parameters.description: No default pattern.

parameters.name: U
parameters.description: A user-defined pattern of simple parallel lines, whose spacing comes from HPSPACE and whose double-hatching comes from HPDOUBLE rather than from HPSCALE.

tools.example:
; Hatch every closed polyline on a layer with a preset pattern
HPNAME ANSI31
HPSCALE 25
HPANG 0

(setq ss (ssget "_X" '((0 . "LWPOLYLINE") (8 . "SECTION") (70 . 1))))
(command "_.-HATCH" "_S" ss "" "")
tools.notes: The pattern must exist in acad.pat or acadiso.pat, or in a custom .pat file found on the support file search path; MEASUREMENT decides which of the two standard files is used. Related: HPSCALE, HPANG, HPASSOC (associativity of new hatches), HPORIGIN (pattern alignment, important for brick and tile), HPGAPTOL (bridging gaps in a boundary), HPLAYER (force new hatches onto a named layer), HPMAXLINES.

tools.name: HPSCALE
tools.description: Default hatch pattern scale for new hatches; it must be greater than zero. It multiplies the pattern definition, so the correct value depends on both the drawing units and the plot scale - a pattern that reads well at 1:1 in millimetres is a solid black smear at 1:100. A script that sets it alongside HPNAME and HPANG gets predictable hatching without touching the dialog.
tools.usage:
HPSCALE <value>
SETVAR HPSCALE 25
(setvar "HPSCALE" 25.0)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "HPSCALE", 25#   ; COM

parameters.description: Multiplier applied to the pattern definition; zero and negative values are rejected.

parameters.name: user-defined patterns
parameters.description: Have no scale - their line spacing comes from HPSPACE and HPDOUBLE instead.

parameters.name: SOLID
parameters.description: Ignores the scale entirely.

tools.example:
; Section hatch sized for a 1:25 sheet
HPNAME ANSI31
HPSCALE 25
HPANG 45
-HATCH

1250,800
tools.notes: A scale that is orders of magnitude too small is the usual cause of the 'hatch spacing too dense' error, whose limit is HPMAXLINES - raise the scale rather than the limit. Annotative hatch patterns take their scale from the annotation scale in CANNOSCALE instead. Related: HPNAME, HPANG, HPSPACE, HPDOUBLE, HPMAXLINES, MEASUREMENT.

tools.name: HPMAXLINES
tools.description: Sets the maximum number of hatch lines that will be generated for a single hatch, from 100 up to 10000000. Exceeding it aborts the hatch with a 'too dense' message rather than locking the session up for minutes while it generates millions of segments, so the limit is a safety net for batch work. Raising it is occasionally justified for a genuinely huge area, but the usual cause is a pattern scale orders of magnitude too small.
tools.usage:
HPMAXLINES <100-10000000>
SETVAR HPMAXLINES 1000000
(setvar "HPMAXLINES" 1000000)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "HPMAXLINES", 1000000   ; COM

parameters.name: 100 to 10000000
parameters.description: Maximum number of lines in one hatch; the default is 1000000.

parameters.name: lower value
parameters.description: Fails fast during unattended batch hatching, which is often what you want in a script that must not hang.

tools.example:
; Guard a batch hatching routine
(setq old-max (getvar "HPMAXLINES"))
(setvar "HPMAXLINES" 200000)
(setvar "HPNAME" "ANSI31")
(setvar "HPSCALE" 25.0)
(command "_.-HATCH" "_S" (ssget "_X" '((0 . "LWPOLYLINE") (70 . 1))) "" "")
(setvar "HPMAXLINES" old-max)
tools.notes: Saved in the registry, so it is a per-user guard rather than a drawing property. A hatch that only just fits under the limit still bloats the file and slows plotting badly - check HPSCALE and the drawing units before raising it. Related: HPNAME, HPSCALE, HPGAPTOL, FILLMODE.

tools.name: ORTHOMODE
tools.description: Constrains cursor movement to the horizontal and vertical axes of the current UCS - the F8 toggle. It affects points picked with the pointing device and distances typed as a bare number in a dragged direction, but not full coordinates, so a script supplying explicit coordinates is unaffected while a macro that relies on direct distance entry depends on it completely. Set it deliberately at the start of a macro rather than trusting whatever the user left it at.
tools.usage:
ORTHOMODE <0 | 1>
SETVAR ORTHOMODE 1
(setvar "ORTHOMODE" 1)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "ORTHOMODE", 1   ; COM

parameters.description: Cursor movement is unconstrained.
Movement is constrained to the X and Y axes of the current UCS.

tools.example:
; Macro that needs orthogonal direct distance entry
(setq old-ortho (getvar "ORTHOMODE"))
(setvar "ORTHOMODE" 1)
(command "_.LINE" pause pause "")
(setvar "ORTHOMODE" old-ortho)
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing. Ortho and polar tracking are mutually exclusive - turning one on turns the other off - so a routine that forces ORTHOMODE 1 silently switches polar tracking off for the user. SNAPANG rotates the axes that ortho follows, which is how ortho works on a rotated grid. Related: OSMODE, SNAPANG, POLARANG.

tools.name: TILEMODE
tools.description: Switches between the Model tab (1) and the last layout tab used (0). Setting it is how a script moves between model space and paper space without clicking a tab, and commands that only make sense in one space - MSPACE, PSPACE, viewport creation, plotting a layout - depend on it being right. Use CTAB when a particular named layout is wanted rather than whichever one was last active.
tools.usage:
TILEMODE <0 | 1>
SETVAR TILEMODE 0
(setvar "TILEMODE" 0)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "TILEMODE", 0   ; COM

parameters.description: The last layout tab becomes current: paper space, with floating viewports.
The Model tab becomes current (the default in a new drawing).

tools.example:
; Go to a layout, work inside a viewport, come back out
(setvar "TILEMODE" 0)
(setvar "CTAB" "A1 - GA PLAN")
(command "_.MSPACE")
(command "_.ZOOM" "_E")
(command "_.PSPACE")
(setvar "TILEMODE" 1)
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing. With TILEMODE 0, MSPACE and PSPACE move the focus in and out of a floating viewport, and CVPORT identifies which viewport is active - setting CVPORT to a viewport's number activates it. Related: CTAB (name of the current tab), LAYOUT and -LAYOUT (create, rename, copy and delete layouts), MODEMACRO and the PSPACE/MSPACE pair.

tools.name: CTAB
tools.description: Holds the name of the current tab: either Model or the name of a layout. Setting it activates that tab, which is the dependable way for a script to reach a particular sheet - safer than setting TILEMODE 0 and hoping the right layout was the last one used. Reading it lets a routine find out where it is running and refuse to draw model geometry on a sheet.
tools.usage:
CTAB <"Model" | "layout name">
SETVAR CTAB "A1 - GA PLAN"
(setvar "CTAB" "A1 - GA PLAN")   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "CTAB", "A1 - GA PLAN"   ; COM

parameters.name: "Model"
parameters.description: Activates the Model tab; equivalent to TILEMODE 1.

parameters.name: layout name
parameters.description: Activates that layout. The name must already exist or the assignment fails; names are not case sensitive and usually contain spaces.

tools.notes: Saved in the drawing. Switching tabs the first time regenerates the layout, which is slow on a heavy drawing - LAYOUTREGENCTL controls how much of that work is cached. -PLOT takes the layout name as an argument of its own, so batch plotting often does not need to switch tabs at all. Related: TILEMODE, LAYOUT, CVPORT.

tools.name: CANNOSCALE
tools.description: Holds the name of the current annotation scale for the current space, as a string such as 1:50 or 1:100. Every annotative object created while it is set supports that scale, and annotative text, dimensions, hatches and blocks size themselves from it instead of from DIMSCALE or a hand-calculated text height. The name must already be in the drawing's scale list - assigning one that is not there fails.
tools.usage:
CANNOSCALE <"scale name">
SETVAR CANNOSCALE 1:50
(setvar "CANNOSCALE" "1:50")   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "CANNOSCALE", "1:50"   ; COM

parameters.name: scale name
parameters.description: The display name of a scale in the drawing's scale list, exactly as SCALELISTEDIT shows it, for example 1:1, 1:50, 1:100.

parameters.name: CANNOSCALEVALUE
parameters.description: The read-only companion that returns the same scale as a number - 0.02 for 1:50 - which is what arithmetic should use.

tools.example:
; Create annotative notes at the sheet scale
CANNOSCALE
1:50
TEXTSTYLE
NOTES-ANNO
TEXT
J
TL
1000,2000
0
GENERAL ARRANGEMENT

; Convert the scale to a factor in LISP
(setvar "CANNOSCALE" "1:50")
(princ (getvar "CANNOSCALEVALUE"))   ; 0.02
tools.notes: Saved in the drawing, separately for model space and for each layout viewport. The scale list is per drawing - -SCALELISTEDIT is the script-safe way to add an entry, and a scale that only exists in one drawing of a set is a common batch failure. Related: CANNOSCALEVALUE (read-only), ANNOALLVISIBLE and ANNOAUTOSCALE (what happens to objects that do not support the current scale), MSLTSCALE, DIMSCALE.

tools.name: SAVETIME
tools.description: Sets the automatic save interval in minutes; 0 turns automatic saving off. The timer restarts whenever the drawing is saved or the value is changed, and the autosave file is written to the folder named by SAVEFILEPATH with an .sv$ extension. A long batch run usually sets it to 0 so that an autosave does not interrupt processing part way through, and restores the user's value at the end.
tools.usage:
SAVETIME <minutes>
SETVAR SAVETIME 0
(setvar "SAVETIME" 0)   ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "SAVETIME", 0   ; COM

parameters.description: Automatic saving is off.
Interval in minutes between automatic saves; the timer counts only while the drawing is modified.

tools.example:
; Batch preamble and restore
(setq old-st (getvar "SAVETIME"))
(setvar "SAVETIME" 0)
(setvar "FILEDIA" 0)
; ... process the drawing ...
(command "_.QSAVE")
(setvar "FILEDIA" 1)
(setvar "SAVETIME" old-st)
tools.notes: Saved in the registry, so it is a per-user setting rather than a drawing property. An automatic save never happens while a command is active, so a routine that leaves a command running blocks it anyway. The .sv$ file is not a substitute for saving - it is removed on a normal exit. Related: SAVEFILE (read-only, the current autosave file name), SAVEFILEPATH, ISAVEPERCENT (how much wasted space is tolerated before a full save), RECOVER and DRAWINGRECOVERY.

tools.name: LASTPOINT
tools.description: Holds the last point entered, expressed in the coordinates of the current UCS. It is what the @ symbol refers to at a coordinate prompt, and unusually for a positional value it can be written as well as read, so a routine can set the base for the next relative entry without drawing anything. Reading it straight after a command is a quick way to recover where that command finished.
tools.usage:
LASTPOINT <x,y,z>
SETVAR LASTPOINT 100,50,0
(setvar "LASTPOINT" (list 100.0 50.0 0.0))   ; AutoLISP - a 3-element list
ActiveDocument.SetVariable "LASTPOINT", pt   ; COM - pt is a 3-element array of doubles

parameters.name: x,y,z
parameters.description: A 3D point in the current UCS. AutoLISP reads and writes it as a list of three reals; COM uses a variant array of three doubles.
Typed at a coordinate prompt, it means this point; @dx,dy and @dist<angle are measured from it.

tools.example:
; Continue a line from wherever the last command finished
(command "_.CIRCLE" '(100 50) 25.0)
(setq p (getvar "LASTPOINT"))
(command "_.LINE" p (polar p 0.0 50.0) "")

; Script form: set the base, then work relative to it
LASTPOINT 0,0,0
LINE
@100,0
@0,50
tools.notes: Not saved between sessions. The value is expressed in the current UCS, so it changes meaning the moment the UCS changes - store it as a WCS point with trans if a routine spans a UCS change. Related: the @ prefix and direct distance entry, ELEV and the current elevation, and (getpoint), which does not update LASTPOINT on its own.

tools.name: DWGNAME
tools.description: Read-only: returns the file name of the current drawing. In current releases it returns the name alone, for example Site-Plan.dwg, with the folder held separately in DWGPREFIX; a drawing that has never been saved returns its temporary name such as Drawing1.dwg. Batch routines use it to build log entries, output file names and title block values.
tools.usage:
DWGNAME                                       ; read-only - typing it displays the value
SETVAR DWGNAME                                ; reports the value; it cannot be set
(getvar "DWGNAME")                            ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.GetVariable("DWGNAME")         ; COM

parameters.name: return value
parameters.description: The file name including the extension; read-only, so any attempt to set it is refused.

parameters.name: unsaved drawings
parameters.description: Return the provisional name (Drawing1.dwg and so on); DWGTITLED is 0 until the drawing has been named by a save.

tools.example:
; Build an export name next to the source drawing
(setq base (vl-filename-base (getvar "DWGNAME")))
(setq out  (strcat (getvar "DWGPREFIX") base ".dxf"))
(setvar "FILEDIA" 0)
(command "_.-EXPORT" "_DXF" "16" out)
(setvar "FILEDIA" 1)
tools.notes: Read-only and not saved. DWGTITLED tells you whether the drawing has ever been saved under a real name (0 = still untitled), which is worth checking before a routine writes files derived from the name. Through COM, ActiveDocument.Name and ActiveDocument.FullName give the same information more directly. Related: DWGPREFIX, SAVENAME, the Filename field available in MTEXT and attributes.

tools.name: DWGPREFIX
tools.description: Read-only: returns the drive and folder of the current drawing, ending in a path separator. Combined with DWGNAME it gives the full path, which is what a batch routine needs in order to write a PDF, a log file or an exported DXF alongside the source drawing. For a drawing that has never been saved it returns the folder the application would default to.
tools.usage:
DWGPREFIX                                     ; read-only - typing it displays the value
SETVAR DWGPREFIX                              ; reports the value; it cannot be set
(getvar "DWGPREFIX")                          ; AutoLISP
ActiveDocument.GetVariable("DWGPREFIX")       ; COM

parameters.name: return value
parameters.description: The folder of the current drawing, with a trailing path separator, so it can be concatenated with a file name directly.

parameters.name: unsaved drawings
parameters.description: Return the default working folder rather than an empty string, so check DWGTITLED before trusting it.

tools.example:
; Plot the current layout to a PDF beside the drawing
(setq pdf (strcat (getvar "DWGPREFIX")
                  (vl-filename-base (getvar "DWGNAME"))
                  ".pdf"))
(princ (strcat "\nPlotting to " pdf))
tools.notes: Read-only and not saved. It returns a native Windows path, so a routine that embeds it in a string literal for another tool may need to translate the separators first. Drawings opened from a network location return the UNC or mapped path as opened. Related: DWGNAME, DWGTITLED, ActiveDocument.Path through COM, and (findfile) for resolving files on the support path instead.

tools.name: ACADVER
tools.description: Read-only: returns the internal version number of the running release as a string, in the form of a major and minor number followed by a suffix. Routines that must behave differently on different releases should test it rather than guessing from the product name, because the major number changes only when a release is not backward compatible. It is not the DWG file format version and not the marketing year of the product.
tools.usage:
ACADVER                                       ; read-only - typing it displays the value
SETVAR ACADVER                                ; reports the value; it cannot be set
(getvar "ACADVER")                            ; AutoLISP
Application.Version                           ; COM - the same number

parameters.name: return value
parameters.description: A string such as 24.3s (LMS Tech): the major version, the minor version, and a build suffix.

parameters.name: comparison
parameters.description: Convert with atof and compare numerically; string comparison gives the wrong answer as soon as the major number reaches double figures.

tools.example:
; Guard a feature that does not exist in older releases
(if (>= (atof (getvar "ACADVER")) 20.1)
  (command "_.SETBYLAYER" "_ALL" "" "_Y" "_Y")
  (princ "\nSETBYLAYER options differ in this release.")
)

; Log the environment at the start of a batch run
(princ (strcat "\n" (getvar "PRODUCT") " " (getvar "ACADVER")))
tools.notes: Read-only and not saved. AutoCAD LT and the vertical products share the same numbering, so it does not identify which application is running - PRODUCT and PROGRAM are the read-only variables for that. The format actually written when the drawing is saved is a separate Save As setting, so never infer the DWG format from this value. Related: PRODUCT, PROGRAM, LOCALE and the Application.Version property through COM.
